how-much-to-charge-to-replaster-a-pool.h.text:
← Pool plaster / resurfacing bid calculator

How much to charge to replaster a pool

The number a homeowner wants is a price per square foot, or a published “$8 plaster special.” That number is usually the water surface: length × width. The plaster goes on the floor and the walls. A 16×32 rectangle with a 3.5-foot shallow end and an 8-foot deep end is 512 square feet of water and about 1,064 square feet of plaster. The pool is still “a 16×32.” The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the walls and the chip-out, not just the water

Pool-route calculators price a weekly chemical stop. Concrete calculators price a slab. Epoxy calculators price a garage floor. A walk-in shower calculator prices tile. A pool replaster is a finish on a shell: the floor, the walls, the finish, the chip-out, the spa, and the tile band. Quoting all of that from a published per-square-foot number written for the water surface is how the first drain-and-chip day eats the field margin.

A job with the same word “plaster” can cost much more

Pebble and glass are billed as their own material and their own hours. Full chip-out to gunite is a different job from a drain-and-overlay. A spa, steps, waterline tile, and coping are adders that get forgotten on a brochure special. On the sample rates a freeform pebble job with full chip-out, an 80-square-foot spa, four benches, 90 feet of tile, and 90 feet of coping prices about $44,058 ($34.56 per plaster square foot, $71.06 per water-surface square foot, 330.1 crew-hours). The same shop’s 16×32 white-plaster overlay prices about $7,826 ($7.36 per plaster square foot, $15.29 per water-surface square foot, 53.4 hours, walk-away $5,791). Matching the brochure job’s water-surface number on the pebble chip-out is how that job becomes a loss.

A 20×40 glass-bead rectangle is not automatically the expensive one per foot of water

A 20×40 glass-bead rectangle with a full chip-out, a 64-square-foot spa, and 80 feet of coping is not the pebble job plus 20%. On the sample rates that pool prices about $58,722 ($35.85 per plaster square foot, 416.0 crew-hours) — more money than the pebble job, but a similar per-plaster-foot number, because the tile band and the freeform wall multiplier do not live in a published water-surface rate. An 18×36 quartz overlay with a 220-square-foot partial chip-out and 70 feet of waterline tile prices about $18,520 (112.3 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first drain day.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $36/h plasterer loaded at 30% payroll burden is $46.80. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a pool specification, a structural determination, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Shell, bond, finish, chip-out, tile, and whether the old plaster will hold a new coat are yours to confirm.

Price your pool replaster

Common questions

How much to charge to replaster a pool?

Charge from floor-plus-wall plaster surface (not length × width), finish, chip-out, spa, steps, waterline tile, coping, drain-and-refill, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 16×32 white-plaster overlay at the sample rates in this calculator prices around $7,826 — about $7.36 per plaster square foot, or $15.29 per square foot of water surface.

Why is a per-square-foot pool plaster quote dangerous?

Homeowners count length × width. The plaster goes on the floor and the walls. Chip-out, pebble or glass finish, a spa, waterline tile, and coping do not scale with the water surface. Matching a cheaper water-surface quote written for a brochure overlay is how a pebble chip-out becomes a two-day loss.

Does a bigger pool always cost more to replaster?

Not in proportion. On the sample rates a freeform pebble job with full chip-out, an 80-square-foot spa, four benches, 90 feet of tile, and 90 feet of coping prices around $44,058 ($35 per plaster square foot), while a 16×32 white-plaster overlay prices around $7,826 ($7.36 per plaster square foot).

Where the hours go

    Where the cost goes

      Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours and material rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a pool specification, or a structural determination — replace them with your own takeoff.

      Hand the customer a proposal

      The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

      Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

      Common questions

      Why does a 16×32 pool come out as 1,064 square feet of plaster?

      Because you plaster the walls, not just the water surface. On the defaults the floor is 512 sq ft (16 × 32) and the walls add another 552 — the perimeter, 96 ft, times the average depth of 5.75 ft, which is the mean of the 3.5 ft shallow end and the 8 ft deep end. That is why a “512 square foot pool” buys a bit over twice that much finish material, and why quoting off water-surface area alone underbuys the job by roughly half.

      Why are there two different per-square-foot prices?

      They divide the same price by two different areas. On the defaults the job prices at $7,825.99, which is $7.36 per plaster square foot (over all 1,064 sq ft of shell) but $15.29 per water square foot (over the 512 sq ft footprint a homeowner would measure). Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. Use the plaster figure to sanity-check your material and labor rates, and the water-surface figure only when you are comparing against a competitor who quoted that way.

      What is the drain-and-refill line actually costing me?

      Two things, and the water is the larger one. The default pool holds about 22,023 gallons (512 sq ft × 5.75 ft average depth × 7.48 gallons per cubic foot), which at $0.012 per gallon is $264.27 of water, plus 3.5 hours of attended drain and refill time. Turning the option off removes both. If your district meters filling differently, or you are on a haul-in rate, that per-gallon field is the one to change.

      Why doesn’t a 26% target margin mean multiplying cost by 1.26?

      Because margin is measured against the price, not against the cost. The default job costs $5,791.23 all in, and holding 26% of the price as profit means dividing by 0.74, not multiplying by 1.26: $5,791.23 ÷ 0.74 = $7,825.99. Marking cost up by 26% would give $7,296.95 and leave you at a 20.6% margin — the single most common way a bid that looked profitable on paper is not.

      Does the price include chip-out?

      Not on the defaults. The chip-out selector starts at “none” — a bond-coat resurface over sound plaster — so the chip-out square footage and its hours are both zero. That is the brochure special most homeowners are comparing against. Switch to partial or full chip-out and both the demolition hours and the dumpster line become real, which is usually the difference between the advertised number and the one you can actually deliver.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-square-foot-of-water..text:
← Pool Plaster Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per square foot of water

“$15 a square foot” is not a price for a pool — it is a price for one specific shell, finish, and scope, quietly charged again for a different job that only looks the same size from the deck.

What a flat rate per square foot of water is

It is the fastest way to quote a replaster: multiply the water surface — length times width, the number a homeowner can read off a tape measure without draining the pool — by a published rate. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer holding a postcard or a cheaper competitor's quote will ask you to match.

It is wrong because the plaster does not stop at the waterline on the floor — it goes up every wall too, and the walls are not part of the water-surface number at all. The rate also does not know which finish or which chip-out it was built for, so the same $-per-square-foot figure gets reused for a bond-coat overlay and a full gunite chip-out with a spa and tile alike.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the shell dimensions, finish, chip-out, spa, steps, waterline tile, coping, and your crew's rates. It converts the shape into a real plaster takeoff — floor plus walls, plus any spa and steps — and returns the price, the price per plaster square foot, the price per water square foot, and the walk-away number below which the job loses money.

What a flat water-surface rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Prices the pool by its water surface — length × width — which is the floor only. Prices the pool by its plaster surface — floor plus walls, spa, and steps — from the shell geometry.
Uses the same $/sq ft whichever finish is chosen, though pebble and glass finishes cost several times more per square foot than white plaster. Prices each finish from its own material cost and labor hours, so a pebble or glass job is billed for the upgrade it actually is.
Has no line for chip-out, so a full demolition to gunite is quoted the same as a bond-coat overlay. Adds chip-out hours and a dumpster line only for the square footage actually billed, separate from the plaster.
Folds a spa, waterline tile, and coping into the same flat rate, or leaves them out. Prices the spa, steps, waterline tile, and coping as their own lines, each visible instead of buried in a bigger, wrong number.
Gives the crew a rate to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price, the price per plaster square foot, the price per water square foot, and the walk-away price, so a shopped rate can be tested against the real job before it goes out.

One rate, two very different pools

Using this calculator's own job presets. A 16×32 rectangle, white plaster, no chip-out — the brochure special — is 512 square feet of water and 1,064 square feet of plaster, and prices at $7,825.99, which works out to $15.29 per square foot of water.

A freeform pebble pool with a full chip-out to gunite, a spa, waterline tile, and coping — the loss job — is 620 square feet of water, not far off the brochure pool's 512. But it is 1,275 square feet of plaster once the walls, spa, and tile band are counted, with a far more expensive finish and a full demolition on top. Matching the brochure job's $15.29-a-square-foot rate to this pool's 620 square feet of water gives a quote of $9,476.79.

This calculator prices the same freeform pebble job at $44,057.94 — a real rate of $71.06 per square foot of water, 4.6 times the brochure job's rate. The flat water-surface quote covers about 21.5% of the real cost, a shortfall of $34,581.15. Nothing about the two pools' water-surface numbers — 512 versus 620, a modest difference — warns that one job is several times the other once the walls, the finish, the chip-out, and the added scope are priced.

Nobody is being careless by reaching for a $-per-square-foot rate first — it is the number that is easiest to compare between bids. The gap is everything a water-surface number cannot see: the walls, the finish, the chip-out, and the extras, which is exactly what this calculator prices and a rate copied from the last job cannot.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per square foot of water surface get pool replastering wrong?

Because the plaster goes on the floor and the walls, and a flat water-surface rate only counts the floor -- length times width. On this calculator's own defaults, a 16×32 rectangle with a 3.5-foot shallow end and an 8-foot deep end is 512 square feet of water but 1,064 square feet of plaster, more than twice as much shell as the water-surface number counts.

How big is the gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own job presets: a 16×32 white-plaster job with no chip-out prices at $7,825.99, which is $15.29 per square foot of water. Applying that same $15.29 rate to a freeform pebble pool with a full chip-out, a spa, waterline tile, and coping -- 620 square feet of water but 1,275 square feet of plaster -- gives a quote of $9,476.79. This calculator prices that job at $44,057.94: the flat water-surface rate covers about 21.5% of the real cost, a $34,581.15 shortfall.

What does pricing by the water surface leave out entirely?

Everything that is not the floor: the walls, which scale with depth and perimeter rather than water area; the finish upgrade, since pebble and glass cost several times more per square foot than white plaster; the chip-out; the spa; waterline tile; and coping. A water-surface rate has no line for any of them, so a pool that looks like a similar size in the number a homeowner can see is priced the same as one that is a several-times larger job in the number that actually gets plastered.

Is pricing by the water surface ever close enough?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- same finish, same chip-out, similar depth and shape -- a flat rate set for one job can land close on the next. The risk is applying a rate learned on a simple brochure job to a pool that looks like a similar size in water surface but carries a deeper shell, a pricier finish, a chip-out, or added scope like a spa or tile, because the water-surface number cannot tell you when that has happened.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates, material costs, or what competitors charge. It takes your shell dimensions, finish, chip-out, and crew rates and turns them into a price built from the actual plaster surface -- the arithmetic a flat water-surface rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat rate per square foot is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the next job stops matching the one the rate was set on.

This calculator vs. Buildxact

Two different shapes: Buildxact is account-based estimating and project-management software for running a construction business across trades and jobs. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this pool replaster cost, given its surface, finish, and chip-out, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Buildxact is construction estimating and project-management software founded in Australia in 2011, with North American headquarters in Austin, Texas. It serves builders, remodelers, and contractors across trades — including carpentry, painting, roofing, and flooring — combining material takeoffs, quoting, job costing, scheduling, and client communication into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Buildxact's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — multi-trade construction estimating and project-management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Buildxact appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Buildxact does. It does not manage takeoffs across trades, schedule crews, track job costs over time, or store any project record on a server. It takes one pool replaster — floor-plus-wall plaster surface (not the homeowner's length times width), finish (white plaster, quartz, pebble, or glass), chip-out scope, a spa, steps, waterline tile, coping, and a drain-and-refill, plus loaded wage, material rates, and target margin — and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, the price per square foot of plaster and of water surface, a breakdown of where the hours and cost actually go, and a copyable customer-facing bid summary, plus a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block.
